en: Itivuttaka 100 Catukkanipāta Brāhmaṇadhammayāgavagga Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of gifts. What four? The gift of material things, the gift of Dhamma, the gift of safety, and the gift of loving-kindness. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of gifts. When this was said, a certain brahmin approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him. When they had concluded their greetings and cordial talk, he sat down to one side and said to the Blessed One: “Master Gotama, what is the difference between one who offers a sacrifice and one who enjoys the fruit of that sacrifice? “There is a case, brahmin, where one person offers a sacrifice, but another enjoys the fruit of that sacrifice. And how is it that one offers a sacrifice, while another enjoys the fruit of that sacrifice? Here, brahmin, someone offers a sacrifice with a mind full of lust, hatred, and delusion; yet another enjoys the fruit of that sacrifice with a mind free from lust, hatred, and delusion. In this way, brahmin, one offers a sacrifice, while another enjoys the fruit of that sacrifice. “But there is also a case, brahmin, where both offer the sacrifice and both enjoy the fruit of that sacrifice. And how is it that both offer the sacrifice and both enjoy the fruit of that sacrifice? Here, brahmin, someone offers a sacrifice with a mind free from lust, hatred, and delusion; and another enjoys the fruit of that sacrifice with a mind free from lust, hatred, and delusion. In this way, brahmin, both offer the sacrifice and both enjoy the fruit of that sacrifice. “Now, brahmin, regarding the offering of a sacrifice: if one offers a sacrifice with a mind full of lust, hatred, and delusion, one does not give oneself as a gift to the devas. But if one offers a sacrifice with a mind free from lust, hatred, and delusion, one gives oneself as a gift to the devas. Therefore, brahmin, one should train thus: ‘We shall offer a sacrifice with a mind free from lust, hatred, and delusion. When this was said, that brahmin said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, Master Gotama! Magnificent, Master Gotama! Just as one might set upright what was overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms, even so has Master Gotama explained the Dhamma in various ways. I go for refuge to Master Gotama, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.”
The Discourse on the Sacrifice of the Dhamma of a Brahmin.
This was said by the Blessed One; having heard it from the mouth of the Blessed One, I have thus retained it:
"Monks, I am a brahmin devoted to sacrifice, with hands always pure, bearing his final body, the unsurpassed physician and surgeon."
To me you are sons born from my breast, born from my mouth, born of the Dhamma, fashioned by the Dhamma, heirs of the Dhamma, not heirs of material things.
Monks, there are these two kinds of gifts:
the gift of material things and the gift of the Dhamma.
“Monks, of these two kinds of giving, this is the foremost: namely, the gift of the Dhamma.
Monks, there are these two kinds of sharing:
the sharing of material things and the sharing of the Dhamma.”
“Monks, of these two kinds of sharing, this is the foremost: namely, the sharing of the Dhamma.
Monks, there are these two kinds of assistance:
assistance with material things and assistance with the Dhamma.”
“Monks, of these two kinds of assistance, this is the foremost: assistance with the Dhamma.
Monks, there are these two kinds of offerings:
the offering of material goods and the offering of the Dhamma.”
“Monks, of these two kinds of sacrifice, this is the foremost: namely, the sacrifice of the Dhamma.
Thus the Blessed One spoke. With reference to this, it is said:
“He who has sacrificed the sacrifice of Dhamma, who is free from stinginess,
the Tathāgata who has compassion for all beings— he such as that,
the best among gods and humans, [is the one worthy of offerings].”
“Beings pay homage to those who have gone beyond existence.
This matter was also spoken by the Blessed One; thus have I heard.
First.
